newsitem.title: USA: Democrats ask U.S. Republicans to produce budget.
newsitem.headline: Democrats ask U.S. Republicans to produce budget.

text.p: Congressional Democratic leaders Wednesday asked Republicans to move on a balanced budget plan before lawmakers leave town for an Easter recess, beginning March 22.
House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle sent a letter to House Speaker Newt Gingrich asking for quick action on a budget plan.
"We call on you to propose your budget plan and begin the process of (writing) a fiscal year 1998 budget resolution before we leave for the upcoming recess," the letter said.

Republican leaders have called on President Clinton to resubmit his five-year balanced budget plan, pointing to new Congressional Budget Office estimates showing it will be $69 billion short of balance in 2002.

Democrats told Republicans to quit sniping at the White House and get down to work on a budget. They warned if Congress did not move quickly, it would be hard to get budget and spending bills passed by the end of the fiscal year.

"In the interest of avoiding a government shutdown, we should get beyond this dispute over who is most accurate in projecting whether the administration's plan balances ... and move immediately to the normal process," the letter said.

Gephardt restated his opposition to an independent commission to recommend changes in the Consumer Price Index, which many experts say overstates inflation. Annual increases in Social Security, Medicare and other benefit programs are based on CPI, so altering it could result in major savings.
Some liberal Democrats worry that the elderly and poor will get lower benefits under the change. Gephardt said that government experts should reassess the inflation measure.
"I think it is a mistake to simply go around the existing process. Once you embroil this in politics, it will defeat your purpose," Gephardt said.
Daschle said that now that the Republican plan for a constitutional amendment to balance the budget had failed, Congress could turn to the real business of cutting government spending.
"The idea that the president should somehow submit a second budget is not only delaying the process, it is politicizing it," Daschle said.
